      WHEN CAST(account_number AS VARCHAR) LIKE '500%'

        THEN '51x_nonpersonnel_operating'
      WHEN CAST(account_number AS VARCHAR) LIKE '59%'
        THEN '59x_financing'
      ELSE 'other_5xx'
    END AS spend_category,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CAST(account_number AS VARCHAR)) AS account_keys,
    SUM(amount) AS adopted_amount
  FROM "analysis_regional_data_6248b76b917ad88fb00a1800"
  WHERE CAST(fund_number AS VARCHAR) = '100000'
    AND lower(trim(budget_cycle)) = 'adopted'
    AND lower(trim(dept_name)) IN ('police', 'commission on police practices')
    AND CAST(account_number AS VARCHAR) LIKE '5%'
    AND (CASE WHEN TRY_CAST(report_fy AS INTEGER) < 100 THEN 2000 + TRY_CAST(report_fy AS INTEGER) ELSE TRY_CAST(report_fy AS INTEGER) END) IN (2024, 2025)
  GROUP BY 1,2,3,4
),
fy24 AS (
  SELECT dept_key, dept_name, spend_category, account_keys, adopted_amount
  FROM base
  WHERE fiscal_year = 2024

  COALESCE(fy25.spend_category, fy24.spend_category) AS spend_category,
  fy24.account_keys AS fy2024_account_keys,
  fy25.account_keys AS fy2025_account_keys,
  fy24.adopted_amount AS fy2024_adopted,
  fy25.adopted_amount AS fy2025_adopted,

 AND fy24.spend_category = fy25.spend_category

synthesis.title: San Diego Police budget dossier: FY2022-FY2023 overtime pressure, uneven unit-level pay variance, and FY2025-FY2026 budget caveats
synthesis.summary: Bounded evidence from City General Fund 100000 expense rows supports several concrete leads. First, Police FY2022 and FY2023 actual 5-prefix expense spending exceeded adopted 5-prefix expense budget, and overtime variance is large enough to be a leading reconciliation target, though not proof of spending above revised legal authority. Second, a blanket vacancy-based explanation does not fit all FY2023 Police funds centers: some 500-series pay centers ended above plan after overtime and related pay are rolled in, while others ended far below plan. Third, budget-to-actual payroll comparisons are structurally distorted because adopted overtime is pooled in budget account 500128 while actual payroll posts to different overtime, holiday, and standby accounts. Fourth, the FY2025 adopted Police increase in these expense rows looks driven mainly by pensions and other compensation, not by overtime. Fifth, the Commission on Police Practices did not show parallel execution or adopted growth in this record set. Sixth, FY2026 Police rows in the current budget export are unlabeled, so this export alone cannot support an 'adopted FY2026' claim. The main gaps are revised appropriations, transfer history, funds-center crosswalks, staffing/vacancy reports, an official account reconciliation, and official FY2026 adoption records.

findings.title: FY2022-FY2023 Police General Fund expense actuals were above adopted expense budget; overtime variance is a leading but unproven explanation
findings.interpretation: Within General Fund 100000 expense accounts beginning with 5, Police actual spending was above adopted in FY2022 and FY2023. Police overtime, defined here by the query as accounts containing "overtime," was also above adopted in both years. That makes overtime a strong place to reconcile the variance, but it does not prove an unauthorized overrun because revised appropriations are not in this record set, and overtime variance alone does not establish the full cause of the department-level gap.
findings.whyItMatters: The key accountability question is not just whether adopted expense rows were exceeded, but whether later legal budget changes, transfers, or staffing conditions explain the difference. Without that reconciliation, public debate can overstate or understate the significance of the over-adopted actuals.
alternativeExplanations: Revised appropriations, transfers, or BAOs may have increased legal authority enough to absorb the adopted-to-actual gap.
Some of the net variance may sit in benefits or other pay lines, with overtime acting only as a correlated symptom.
One-time events, backfill needs, or labor-timing effects could have raised overtime without indicating a chronic budgeting problem.
findings.nextTest: Obtain FY2022-FY2023 revised Police appropriations, transfer history, and year-end legal budget reports for General Fund 100000. This interpretation would be weakened or disproved if revised authority fully covered the adopted-to-actual gap or if a formal variance report shows non-overtime accounts, not overtime, drove the net difference.

findings.title: A department-wide vacancy explanation does not fit all FY2023 Police funds centers
findings.interpretation: The FY2023 500-series comparability test is mixed across Police funds centers. Center 1914121117 shows a positive total 500-series variance driven by overtime and related pay despite only a small regular-pay underrun. Center 1914121111 also ended above its total 500-series budget, and its regular-pay subtotal exceeded the budget subtotal even though the adopted budget included a large negative "Budgeted Personnel Expenditure Savings" line. But center 1914180011 ended far below its 500-series budget, mainly because actual overtime and related pay were far below plan. This weakens any one-size-fits-all story that vacancies alone explain Police pay variance across units.
findings.whyItMatters: If the pressure is concentrated in particular funds centers rather than spread evenly across Police, then department-wide narratives may hide unit-specific operational stress, unrealistic savings assumptions, or misallocated overtime planning.
alternativeExplanations: Funds centers may represent very different functions, so their pay patterns may not be comparable without a service crosswalk.
Some centers may have been designated backfill or specialty-workload hubs that were expected to use more overtime.
The adopted personnel-savings assumptions may have been unusually aggressive in some centers, making actual pay look high even if managers behaved as expected.
findings.nextTest: Get a funds-center-to-unit crosswalk plus monthly FY2023 budgeted positions, filled positions, separations, overtime hours, and backfill logs for centers 1914121117, 1914121111, and 1914180011. This interpretation would be weakened if those centers prove not comparable, or if detailed staffing and deployment records show the over-plan centers were intentionally budgeted as overtime-heavy service hubs.

findings.title: Budgeted overtime and actual payroll post to different account structures, so raw row-matching can mislead
findings.interpretation: Police adopted budget rows pool overtime planning in account 500128 "Overtime Budgeted," while actual payroll posts mainly to 500124 "Overtime - Premium" and 500133 "Overtime - Comp," with additional actual-only holiday and standby-type pay lines. That means a simple account-by-account join will manufacture many apparent "missing actual" or "missing budget" variances that are accounting-structure differences rather than proof of management failure.
findings.whyItMatters: Any serious Police overtime analysis needs an official crosswalk or a defensible rollup. Without that, an analyst can overstate unbudgeted overtime or mistake a chart-of-accounts design issue for a spending-control problem.

findings.title: The FY2025 adopted Police increase in these expense rows was driven more by pensions and other compensation than by overtime
findings.interpretation: Between adopted FY2024 and adopted FY2025, Police General Fund 5-prefix expense rows increased by 50,093,384. The category rollup shows large increases in 502 benefits/pensions and 500 pay other, while the 500 pay overtime/holiday/standby category decreased. On this bounded evidence, the increase looks more like a structural compensation and pension commitment than an overtime catch-up.
findings.whyItMatters: If the biggest adopted Police increase was not mainly overtime, then the budget debate should focus on recurring compensation costs, pension growth, and staffing assumptions rather than treating the increase as a temporary overtime fix.
alternativeExplanations: The pension increase may mainly reflect actuarial or rate changes rather than a discretionary expansion of policing service.
Regular-pay growth may reflect labor agreements, step increases, reduced vacancy assumptions, or filled positions rather than new service commitments.
Some service-expansion costs could sit in categories not isolated by this rollup.
findings.nextTest: Get the FY2025 Police budget build-up showing pension-rate effects, labor-settlement costs, position changes, and vacancy-factor changes. This interpretation would be weakened if official budget support shows the net increase was primarily driven by service additions or other categories outside the compensation-heavy rollup used here.

findings.title: The Commission on Police Practices did not show parallel execution or adopted growth in this record set
findings.interpretation: In the same General Fund 5-prefix expense scope, the Commission on Police Practices spent far below adopted in FY2022 and FY2023, and its adopted FY2025 total was slightly below FY2024. On this bounded record, a claim that police oversight scaled up in parallel with Police spending is not supported. The reason remains unresolved.
findings.whyItMatters: Oversight capacity is often discussed alongside Police funding. If the oversight body was not executing its adopted budget and then did not receive a higher adopted total, the next step is to determine whether that reflects vacancies and delayed build-out or a substantive priority gap.
alternativeExplanations: The Commission may have faced vacancies, start-up delays, or phased implementation rather than an intentional funding deprioritization.
Some oversight-related costs may have been booked outside the Commission's own General Fund 5-prefix rows.
The small FY2025 total decline may coexist with internal rebalancing toward personnel.
findings.nextTest: Obtain FY2022-FY2025 Commission staffing, vacancy, hiring, and quarterly expenditure records. This interpretation would be weakened if those records show the apparent under-execution mainly reflects delayed hiring, or if major oversight costs were carried elsewhere in City accounts.

findings.title: The FY2026 budget export cannot by itself support an 'adopted Police budget' claim
findings.interpretation: The current export shows FY2026 budget rows only under an unlabeled cycle, and raw Police FY2026 rows carry blank cycle fields. On this evidence alone, FY2026 Police amounts in the export should not be treated as confirmed adopted commitments.
findings.whyItMatters: A budget claim can fail on source status alone. Before comparing FY2026 Police figures to homelessness, sanitation, or oversight spending, the adoption status of the FY2026 rows has to be verified from an official ordinance or clearly labeled export.
alternativeExplanations: The City may have adopted FY2026 elsewhere, and the blank cycle may be only an export or ingestion defect.
Another official file may identify these same Police rows as proposed or adopted even though this extract does not.
findings.nextTest: Verify FY2026 Police figures against the adopted ordinance or an official budget file with a populated cycle/status field. This interpretation would be disproved if an official adopted record matches these blank-cycle rows and identifies them as adopted FY2026 amounts.
